mainTopic: A גוי's pouring and mixing of wine (כחו שלא בכוונה, the fence of the נזיר), and ריש לקיש's rulings in בצרה
overview: The amud opens in the middle of a story about רבנן who had a גוי pour drinks for them. One opinion forbade the drink, because the גוי would assume great רבנן drink wine and may have offered it to his idol. The other opinion permitted it, because the גוי would assume רבנן would never ask a non-Jew to pour wine, so it must be beer. The גמרא defends the permitting view against three questions. He could not see it because it was night. He could not smell it because it was new wine. He did not touch it, because he only poured it, and the רבנן made no decree about כחו שלא בכוונה. Next, רבי אסי asks רבי יוחנן about wine a גוי mixed with water. After a short exchange about the right word (לשון תורה לעצמה, לשון חכמים לעצמו), רבי יוחנן forbids it as a fence, like a נזיר who is told to stay away from the vineyard. A story about רבי ירמיה and a formal statement confirm this ruling. Finally, ריש לקיש forbids untithed fruit and worshipped water in בצרה, and רבי יוחנן tells him to take back both rulings: בצרה is not the Torah's בצר, and public water cannot become forbidden. The amud ends by noting that רבי יוחנן is following his own reasoning, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Why the one who forbade was right
steps.stepSummary: The גוי assumes great רבנן would only drink wine, so he may have offered it to his idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: The non-Jew says to himself: 'Could it be that great Rabbis like these are drinking beer? It must be wine.' So he may have poured some of it as an offering to his idol.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning of the one who forbade the drink. It is the גוי's own assumption that makes it a problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is what the גוי thought he was pouring. If he believed it was wine, he might have quietly offered it to his idol (ניסוך), which makes it forbidden. Great רבנן seem too important to drink plain beer, so he would assume it was wine.

keyTerms.meaning: He poured it as an offering to idols
Could it enter your mind? (a way of saying 'impossible!')

phrases.english: He says to himself:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the non-Jew who poured the drinks in the story the גמרא just told.

phrases.english: Could it enter one's mind that Rabbis
like these are drinking beer?
Rather, this is surely wine,
and so he poured it as an idolatrous offering.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵימָר אָמַר: סָלְקָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ דְּרַבָּנַן כִּי הָנֵי שִׁיכְרָא קָא שָׁתוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי יהושע בן לוי's explanation of the forbidding opinion, which began just before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The drink was forbidden because the גוי would have assumed it was wine and may have offered it to his idol.

steps.title: Why the one who permitted was right
steps.stepSummary: The גוי assumes רבנן would never ask a non-Jew to pour wine, so it must be beer, and he did not offer it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who permitted was also right. The non-Jew says to himself: 'Could it be that Rabbis like these are drinking wine and telling me, a non-Jew, "Come pour for us"? It must be beer.' So he did not offer it to his idol.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the opposite reasoning, for the one who permitted the drink.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This side uses the same kind of thinking but reaches the other answer. The גוי knows that Jews keep away from wine a non-Jew handles. If the רבנן were happy to let him pour, it must not be wine, so he had no reason to offer it.

phrases.english: The one who permitted permitted properly,
for he says to himself:
Could it enter your mind that Rabbis
like these are drinking wine,
and they say to me,
'Come, pour drinks for us'?
Rather, it is surely beer
(that they are drinking), and so he did not offer it.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets; the meaning stays the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite opinion's reasoning, built the same way as step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The drink was permitted because the גוי would have assumed it was beer, so he had no reason to offer it.

steps.title: Couldn't the non-Jew just see it was wine?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the permitting view: the גוי can see what he is pouring.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the permitting view. Why would the גוי have to guess when he could simply look at the drink?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The permitting view depends on the גוי not knowing it was wine. If he could see it was wine, his guess about the רבנן would not matter.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so that... (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: But he sees it!

steps.kashyaTarget: The permitting view's claim that the גוי thought it was beer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Anyone pouring a drink can see whether it is wine.

steps.title: It was at night
steps.stepSummary: It happened at night, so he could not see what it was.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the story happened in the dark.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the dark, the גוי could not tell wine from beer by looking. So he still had to rely on his guess about the רבנן.

phrases.english: At night.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גוי could see that it was wine.
steps.terutzMaskana: It was dark, so he could not see.

steps.title: Couldn't he smell it was wine?
steps.stepSummary: Even in the dark, he can smell wine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes again. Even if he could not see, wine has a smell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The darkness answer only removes sight. Smell could still tell him it was wine, which would bring back the problem.

phrases.english: But he smells it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge, after step 4's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the גוי did not know it was wine
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Wine's smell would tell him what it was even in the dark.

steps.title: It was new wine
steps.stepSummary: New wine does not give off a strong smell.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the wine was new, so its smell was too weak to notice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wine that is still new does not yet have a strong smell. So he could neither see nor smell that it was wine.

phrases.english: With new wine.
phrases.notes: New wine doesn't give off much smell yet.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: He would recognize the wine by its smell.

steps.title: He touched the wine with the pail
steps.stepSummary: Even without offering it, his unintentional touch should forbid the wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he touched the wine with the pail, so it is a non-Jew's unintentional touch, and that is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a different problem. Leave aside whether he offered it; he physically touched the wine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a touch with no plan to offer the wine (מגע גוי שלא בכוונה) makes wine forbidden to drink. So even if the גוי thought it was beer, drawing it with a pail should still forbid it.

keyTerms.meaning: A pail or ladle used to draw liquid

phrases.english: But he touched it with the pail,
so it is a non-Jew's touch
without intention, which is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new kind of challenge. It no longer asks what the גוי knew; it asks about his physical touch.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even an unintentional touch by a גוי forbids wine, so his intention does not matter.

steps.title: He only poured it, and there is no decree on that
steps.stepSummary: He poured from one vessel to another without touching it, which is כחו שלא בכוונה, and the רבנן made no decree about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the case is where he poured from one vessel into another. That is his force without intention, and the Rabbis made no decree about any case of force without intention.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the גוי never touched the wine. He only poured it, and that kind of action was never forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא separates touching (מגע) from moving wine by pouring it (כחו, his force). An unintentional touch forbids the wine. When wine moves only through the גוי's force and he has no intention of offering it, the רבנן did not make a decree, so the wine stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this case
Pouring from one vessel into another

steps.whatToRemember: A גוי's unintentional touch forbids wine. But wine moved only by his force, with no intention of offering it (כחו שלא בכוונה), is not forbidden, because the רבנן made no decree about it.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up מגע שלא בכוונה (touching without intention), which IS forbidden, with כחו שלא בכוונה (pouring without touching and without intention), which is NOT.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out a general rule for wine handled by a גוי: the difference between touching it directly and moving it by pouring.

phrases.english: No, it is needed only
where he was pouring from vessel to vessel,
so it is his force without intention,
and any case of his force without intention,
the Rabbis did not decree about it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 7 and closes the discussion of the story.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case plus a general legal rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גוי touched the wine directly with a pail.
steps.terutzMaskana: He only poured it, and the רבנן did not decree about כחו שלא בכוונה.

steps.title: רבי אסי asks about wine a non-Jew mixed
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי asks רבי יוחנן what the law is for wine that a גוי mixed with water.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי asked רבי יוחנן: wine that a non-Jew mixed (with water), what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רבי אסי asks a halachic question, using the word מסכו for 'mixed'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is about a גוי who mixes water into wine. The word רבי אסי chooses will become the focus of the next few lines.

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אַסִּי מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Asi asked Rabbi Yochanan:
Wine that a non-Jew mixed, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַבִּי אַסִּי מֵרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether wine that a גוי mixed with water is permitted

steps.title: רבי יוחנן objects to the word 'מסכו'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן asks why רבי אסי did not use the usual word, מזגו.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Why not say 'diluted' (מזגו)?
steps.whatsHappening: Before answering, רבי יוחנן challenges the wording of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מזג is the ordinary word the חכמים use for mixing wine with water. רבי יוחנן questions why רבי אסי used an unusual word instead.

keyTerms.meaning: Diluted it (the usual word for mixing wine with water)

phrases.english: He said to him: Why not say 'diluted it'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording of the question in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אסי's use of the word מסכו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The usual word for this is מזגו, so why use a different one?

steps.title: רבי אסי: I'm using the word from the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי defends his word by quoting משלי, where מסכה is used for mixing wine.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am speaking the way it is written: 'She has prepared her meat, she has mixed her wine.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אסי answers that his word comes straight from a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He shows that מסך is a real word for mixing wine, found in תנ"ך. So he argues his wording is correct.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am speaking as it is written,
'She has slaughtered her meat, she has mixed her wine.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends against the challenge in step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: מסכו is an odd word to use.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is the word used in the פסוק.

steps.title: The Torah's language is separate from the חכמים' language
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן replies that words in תנ"ך don't decide how the חכמים speak.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The language of the Torah is its own, and the language of the Sages is its own.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן turns down רבי אסי's proof from the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A word used in תנ"ך is not necessarily the word the חכמים use. When asking a halachic question, you should use the חכמים' term, which is מזג.
steps.whatToRemember: לשון תורה לעצמה, לשון חכמים לעצמו: the חכמים have their own vocabulary, and it is not always the same as the words in the פסוקים.

phrases.english: He said to him: The language of the Torah is its own,
and the language of the Sages is its own.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְשׁוֹן תּוֹרָה לְעַצְמָהּ, לְשׁוֹן חֲכָמִים לְעַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the פסוק to justify the word; it does not deny that the word appears in the פסוק.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: תנ"ך's vocabulary does not decide the terms the חכמים use.

steps.title: Wine mixed by a non-Jew is forbidden as a safeguard
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי asks his question again, and רבי יוחנן answers that the wine is forbidden, using the saying about a נזיר who must keep away from the vineyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: [רבי אסי asked:] What is the law? [רבי יוחנן] said to him: It is forbidden, because of the saying: 'Go, go, we tell the נזיר; go around, go around, do not come near the vineyard.'
steps.whatsHappening: After the side discussion about the word מסכה, רבי אסי repeats his question. רבי יוחנן answers that the wine is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גוי did not touch the wine, so you might think it stays permitted. רבי יוחנן forbids it anyway as a fence. A נזיר is only forbidden to eat grape products, yet he is told to stay away from the vineyard itself. In the same way, the חכמים keep a Jew far away from wine a גוי handled.

keyTerms.meaning: a נזיר, who may not drink wine or eat grapes
go around, go around (keep your distance)

steps.whyThisMatters: The saying about the נזיר is a classic source for the idea of making a fence, a גזירה that keeps a person far from a real איסור.

phrases.english: What [is the law]?
phrases.notes: רבי אסי is going back to the question he asked before the argument about the word מסכה.

phrases.english: He said to him: It is forbidden,
because of: 'Go, go, we say to a נזיר;
phrases.notes: This is a well-known saying. A נזיר may not eat grapes, so we tell him to stay away from the vineyard altogether.

phrases.english: go around, go around, do not come near the vineyard.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the side argument about wording in steps 10-12, this step goes back to the question from step 9 and answers it.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Wine a גוי mixed with water is forbidden by a fence-type גזירה, like a נזיר who is kept away from the vineyard.

steps.title: רבי ירמיה forbids mixed wine in סבתא
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה saw Jews drinking wine that גוים had mixed, and he forbade it for the same reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה came to the town of סבתא. He saw wine that גוים had mixed with water, and a Jew drank from it. He forbade it to them because of the saying: 'Go, go, we tell the נזיר; go around, go around, do not come near the vineyard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life story in which רבי ירמיה acted on this exact ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story shows the ruling was not just theory. A רב actually used it in practice, for the same reason רבי יוחנן gave.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya happened to come to Savta,
he saw wine that gentiles had mixed [with water]
and a Jew drank from it,
and he forbade it to them
because of: 'Go, go, we say to a נזיר;
go around, go around, do not come near the vineyard.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up רבי יוחנן's ruling with a story of it being used in practice.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling that wine mixed by a גוי is forbidden

steps.title: A formal statement of the same ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a formal statement in the name of רבי יוחנן (or רבי אסי quoting him) that wine mixed by a גוי is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also stated: רבי יוחנן said, and some say רבי אסי said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Wine that a גוי mixed is forbidden, because of the saying: 'Go, go, we tell the נזיר; go around, go around, do not come near the vineyard.'
steps.whatsHappening: Using the words אתמר נמי, the גמרא shows that this ruling was also passed down as an official teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling now appears as a set teaching, not only as an answer in a conversation. There is a small doubt about who said it, רבי יוחנן himself or רבי אסי quoting him. Either way, it comes from רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: it was also stated (a formal teaching that supports what came before)

steps.whatToRemember: Wine a גוי mixed with water, even without touching it, is forbidden as a fence, just as a נזיר is kept away from the vineyard.

phrases.english: It was also stated:
Rabbi Yochanan said,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: and some say Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
Wine that a gentile mixed is forbidden,
because of: 'Go, go, we say to a נזיר;
go around, go around, do not come near the vineyard.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives formal support to the ruling from steps 13-14 and closes this topic.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling that wine mixed by a גוי is forbidden
steps.raayaSupportSource: An official statement of רבי יוחנן (or רבי אסי in his name)

steps.title: ריש לקיש forbids things in בצרה
steps.stepSummary: In בצרה, ריש לקיש forbade untithed fruit that Jews were eating, and also water that גוים bowed to.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש came to בצרה. He saw Jews eating fruit that had not been tithed, and he forbade it to them. He saw water that גוים bowed down to, and Jews were drinking it, and he forbade it to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story. ריש לקיש makes two rulings in the town of בצרה, and the next step will look at them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate rulings here. One is about the fruit: he treated it as needing מעשר. The other is about the water: he treated water that was worshipped as forbidden. This sets up רבי יוחנן's answer in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: fruit that has not been tithed

phrases.english: Reish Lakish happened to come to Botzra,
he saw Jews who were eating
fruit that was not tithed, and he forbade it to them.
He saw water that gentiles bowed down to
and Jews drank it, and he forbade it to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new story with two new rulings, about מעשר and about worshipped water.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש forbade the untithed fruit of בצרה and the water that גוים worshipped.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן tells ריש לקיש to take back both rulings
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן tells ריש לקיש to go back right away and cancel his rulings. בצרה is not the Torah's בצר, and public water cannot become forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: [ריש לקיש] came before רבי יוחנן. He said to him: While your coat is still on you, go back and retract! בצר is not the same as בצרה, and water that belongs to the public does not become forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן rejects both of ריש לקיש's rulings and tells him to fix them right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On the fruit: ריש לקיש mixed up בצרה with בצר, a city named in the Torah. בצרה is a different place, so its fruit does not need מעשר. On the water: water that belongs to the public cannot become forbidden, even if גוים worship it.

keyTerms.meaning: while your coat is still on you (act right away)
בצר, a city named in the Torah

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up בֶּצֶר and בׇּצְרָה. They sound alike, but רבי יוחנן's whole point is that they are two different places.
steps.whatToRemember: Fruit of בצרה does not need מעשר, because it is not the Torah's בצר. Public water does not become forbidden even if גוים bow to it.

phrases.english: He came before Rabbi Yochanan,
he said to him: While your coat is still on you,
phrases.notes: He means: act right away, before you even take your coat off.

phrases.english: go back [and retract your rulings].
Betzer is not the same as Botzra,
phrases.notes: בצר is a city named in דברים 4:43.

phrases.english: and water belonging to the public does not become forbidden.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Both rulings: the one on the fruit and the one on the water
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: בצרה was wrongly treated as the Torah's בצר, and public water cannot become forbidden through worship.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן follows his own reasoning
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבי יוחנן's ruling about the public water fits his usual line of reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן is following his own reasoning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that רבי יוחנן's ruling in Step 17 matches how he thinks elsewhere. This is a setup line; the continuation on the next amud shows where his consistent view comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 17, רבי יוחנן ruled that public water cannot become forbidden even if גוים bowed to it. The phrase לטעמיה tells us this is not a one-time ruling but part of a steady position he holds. The גמרא is preparing to bring his other statement as support.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning; consistent with his usual view

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this line finishes the point by itself. It only announces that a matching statement of רבי יוחנן is coming next.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan is following his own reasoning,
phrases.notes: This points back to his ruling in Step 17, that public water cannot become forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects רבי יוחנן's ruling in Step 17 to his broader consistent position, setting up a supporting source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן's ruling that public water does not become forbidden matches his usual reasoning, which the גמרא is about to show.
